reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Defined clinically by the number, size and distribution of serrated polyps rather than by a single causative gene, and most cases lack an identified germline mutation
Diagnosis rests on established polyp-count and size criteria, such as multiple serrated polyps proximal to the rectum or a high cumulative lifetime polyp count
Confers an increased risk of colorectal cancer, which arises through the serrated neoplasia pathway rather than the classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence
Serrated lesions, especially sessile serrated lesions in the proximal colon, are flat and pale and easily missed, so high-quality colonoscopy with meticulous inspection is essential
First-degree relatives of affected individuals have a raised colorectal cancer risk and warrant earlier and more frequent colonoscopic screening
Management is regular colonoscopic surveillance with clearance of significant polyps, and surgery is reserved for uncontrollable polyp burden or malignancy
The serrated pathway is frequently associated with BRAF mutation, CpG island methylation and, in some tumours, acquired mismatch-repair deficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Serrated polyposis reflects dysregulation of the serrated neoplasia pathway, a route to colorectal cancer distinct from the conventional adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Sessile serrated lesions commonly carry activating BRAF mutations and develop widespread promoter hypermethylation known as the CpG island methylator phenotype, which silences tumour-suppressor and repair genes. Epigenetic silencing of a mismatch-repair gene in some lesions leads to acquired microsatellite instability, driving progression from serrated polyp to carcinoma; while the condition clusters in families, a consistent germline determinant has not been established for most patients.
additionalDifferentials: Familial adenomatous polyposis and its attenuated form
additionalInvestigations: High-quality colonoscopy with careful proximal-colon inspection and documentation of polyp number, size and location against diagnostic criteria
Histopathological classification of serrated lesions, including sessile serrated lesions and traditional serrated adenomas
Molecular testing of tumours for BRAF mutation and CpG island methylation where relevant
Mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry on carcinomas to detect acquired deficiency
Consideration of germline multigene panel testing when features suggest another syndrome
Colonoscopic screening of first-degree relatives at an earlier age
redFlags: A large or endoscopically complex serrated lesion suspicious for malignancy
A discrete mass or advanced histology on biopsy
Rapidly increasing polyp burden that cannot be cleared endoscopically
reference.prognosis: With diligent colonoscopic surveillance and complete removal of significant serrated lesions, colorectal cancer risk can be well controlled and prognosis is good. Risk persists lifelong and depends on the completeness of examinations, so meticulous ongoing surveillance and family screening are important.
pitfalls: Missing flat, pale sessile serrated lesions in the proximal colon during suboptimal colonoscopy
Dismissing hyperplastic-appearing polyps without recognising the cumulative diagnostic criteria
Failing to screen first-degree relatives at increased colorectal cancer risk
Assuming a germline mutation must be present and stopping surveillance when testing is negative
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment - Colorectal
management: Undertake regular colonoscopic surveillance with complete endoscopic clearance of significant serrated polyps as the mainstay of management
Ensure high-quality colonoscopy with meticulous proximal-colon inspection, adequate bowel preparation, and image-enhancement techniques to detect flat, pale sessile serrated lesions
Reserve surgery such as colectomy for an uncontrollable polyp burden or established malignancy
Classify serrated lesions histopathologically and perform mismatch-repair immunohistochemistry on any carcinoma to detect acquired deficiency
Screen first-degree relatives colonoscopically at an earlier age given their raised colorectal cancer risk
Consider germline multigene panel testing when features suggest an alternative hereditary syndrome
Advise lifestyle risk reduction including smoking cessation as an adjunct to surveillance
